subject: Chemistry
title: How Fireworks Get Their Colors
description: A 60-second lesson on How Fireworks Get Their Colors.

hook.text: Every firework color comes from a different metal salt burning at thousands of degrees in midair.

buildup.text: A firework shell contains gunpowder for lift, a fuse for timing, and 'stars'—pellets of metal salts.

discovery.text: Strontium compounds burn red. Barium burns green. Copper burns blue. Sodium burns bright yellow.

twist.text: Blue is the hardest color. Copper chloride decomposes at the temperature needed to see it, so the timing must be perfect.

climax.text: White comes from magnesium or aluminum. Gold from charcoal and iron. Chemistry paints the sky.

punchline.text: Metal salts in the sky. Each element burns its own color.

quiz.question: Why is blue the hardest firework color to produce?
options: The copper compound decomposes at the temperatures needed to excite it
Blue dye is the most expensive
Human eyes can't see blue well at night

details.summary: Fireworks produce colors when metal salts are heated to high temperatures, causing their electrons to jump to excited energy states and then emit photons of specific wavelengths as they fall back down. Strontium produces red, barium gives green, copper creates blue, and sodium yields bright yellow.
details.whyItMatters: Firework chemistry is a practical application of atomic emission spectra, the same principle used in spectroscopy to identify elements in unknown samples and distant stars.
takeaways: Different metal salts produce characteristic colors when heated
Electron transitions between energy levels emit specific wavelengths
Creating a good blue firework is the most chemically challenging color

faq.question: Why is blue the hardest firework color to produce?
faq.answer: Blue requires copper compounds that emit at a narrow wavelength range around 450 nanometers. At the high temperatures needed for bright emission, these copper compounds tend to decompose. Finding compounds that remain stable while producing intense blue light is a persistent pyrotechnic challenge.

faq.question: How do fireworks produce white light and sparkle effects?
faq.answer: White is produced by burning metals like magnesium, aluminum, or titanium at very high temperatures. These metals emit across a broad spectrum. Sparkle effects come from larger metal particles that burn individually at different rates, creating distinct points of light rather than a uniform glow.
